title: Experiment Tracking with MLflow and Weights & Biases
summary: When you train dozens of models with different settings, memory alone cannot track what worked. Experiment tracking tools like MLflow and Weights & Biases automatically log parameters, metrics, and artifacts, giving you dashboards to compare runs and
content:
# Experiment Tracking with MLflow and Weights & Biases ##### The best model that could not be found again A team spent three weeks tuning a fraud detection model. On a Thursday afternoon, one run hit 0.91 F1 — a substantial improvement over the 0.84 baseline. Somebody screenshotted the terminal output and posted it in Slack. The following week they needed to deploy it. Nobody could reproduce the result. The notebook had been modified since. The learning rate in the screenshot was visible, but the feature set was not — and three feature engineering variants had been tried that week. The random seed had been changed at some point. The data file had been regenerated on Friday. Four people had been running experiments on the same notebook. They never recovered the 0.91 configuration. Two weeks of work reconstructing it got them to 0.88, and the team quietly moved on. Sculley et al. (2015) named this category of problem **hidden technical debt in machine learning systems** — the maintenance burden that accumulates when ML code is treated as scripts rather than software. Experiment tracking is one of the cheapest fixes available: a few lines per run, and every experiment becomes permanently reproducible. ##### Why memory and spreadsheets fail The obvious alternatives break down quickly. **Terminal output** disappears when you close the window, and scrolling back through 200 epochs of logs to compare two runs is impractical. **Manual spreadsheets** work for about a week. Then you forget an entry, or record the hyperparameters but not the data version, or two people update it simultaneously. **Filenames** — `model_lr001_depth5_v3_final_ACTUAL.pkl` — encode a few parameters and omit the rest, and they do not tell you what score the model achieved. The core problem is that an ML experiment has **many more inputs than you think**: hyperparameters, feature set, data version, preprocessing choices, random seed, library versions, hardware, and the code itself. Reproducing a result means reproducing all of them, and a screenshot captures perhaps three. ##### What to log for every run This is the assignment's second question, and the list is worth internalizing: | Category | Examples | |---|---| | **Parameters** | Learning rate, batch size, model type, depth, regularization | | **Metrics** | Train and validation loss, accuracy, F1, AUC — per epoch | | **Data** | Dataset version or hash, row count, split ratios, class balance | | **Code** | Git commit hash, whether the working tree was dirty | | **Environment** | Python and library versions, hardware | | **Artifacts** | The model file, plots, confusion matrix, feature importances | | **Metadata** | Run name, tags, who ran it, how long it took | The two most commonly omitted are **data version** and **git commit** — and they are the two that made the 0.91 unreproducible. Logging them costs two lines. ##### MLflow MLflow is open source, runs locally with no account, and stores everything in a local directory or a database. It is the pragmatic default. ```python import mlflow import mlflow.sklearn import subprocess from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, roc_auc_score, classification_report mlflow.set_tracking_uri("file:./mlruns") # or a remote server mlflow.set_experiment("fraud-detection") def git_info() -> dict: """Capture exactly which code produced this run.""" try: commit = subprocess.check_output( ["git", "rev-parse", "HEAD"], text=True).strip() dirty = bool(subprocess.check_output( ["git", "status", "--porcelain"], text=True).strip()) return {"git_commit": commit, "git_dirty": dirty} except subprocess.CalledProcessError: return {"git_commit": "unknown", "git_dirty": True} with mlflow.start_run(run_name="rf-baseline") as run: params = { "model_type": "RandomForest", "n_estimators": 300, "max_depth": 12, "min_samples_leaf": 5, "class_weight": "balanced", "random_state": 42, } mlflow.log_params(params) # The context that makes it reproducible mlflow.log_params({ **git_info(), "data_version": data_hash, # hash of the training file "n_train": len(X_train), "n_features": X_train.shape[1], "positive_rate": float(y_train.mean()), }) mlflow.set_tags({"stage": "experiment", "author": "ananya"}) model = RandomForestClassifier(**{k: v for k, v in params.items() if k != "model_type"}) model.fit(X_train, y_train) y_pred = model.predict(X_val) y_prob = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1] mlflow.log_metrics({ "f1": f1_score(y_val, y_pred), "roc_auc": roc_auc_score(y_val, y_prob), "train_f1": f1_score(y_train, model.predict(X_train)), }) # Artifacts: anything you would want to inspect later mlflow.log_text(classification_report(y_val, y_pred), "classification_report.txt") fig = plot_confusion_matrix(y_val, y_pred) mlflow.log_figure(fig, "confusion_matrix.png") mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, "model", signature=mlflow.models.infer_signature(X_train, y_pred), input_example=X_train[:3]) print(f"Run ID: {run.info.run_id}") ``` Then `mlflow ui` opens a local dashboard at `localhost:5000` where you can sort runs by metric, compare parameters side by side, and view artifacts. The **model signature** is worth including — it records the expected input schema and output type, so loading the model later tells you exactly what columns it wants. That prevents a common deployment failure where feature order silently differs. Logging **per-epoch metrics** gives you learning curves in the dashboard: ```python for epoch in range(n_epochs): train_loss = train_one_epoch(...) val_loss, val_acc = evaluate(...) mlflow.log_metrics({"train_loss": train_loss, "val_loss": val_loss, "val_acc": val_acc}, step=epoch) ``` **Autologging** captures most of this automatically for supported libraries: ```python mlflow.sklearn.autolog() # or mlflow.pytorch, mlflow.tensorflow, mlflow.xgboost ``` It is a good starting point, but add your own data version, git commit and custom metrics — autolog cannot know about those. ##### The model registry Tracking records experiments; the **registry** manages which model is production. ```python result = mlflow.register_model(f"runs:/{run_id}/model", "fraud-detector") client = mlflow.MlflowClient() client.set_registered_model_alias("fraud-detector", "champion", version=result.version) client.set_model_version_tag("fraud-detector", result.version, "validated_by", "ananya") # Loading in production by alias, not version number model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/fraud-detector@champion") ``` Using an **alias** rather than a hard-coded version number means promoting a new model is a registry change rather than a code deployment. It also makes rollback immediate — point the alias back at the previous version. ##### Weights & Biases W&B is a hosted service with a stronger dashboard and better collaboration, free for personal and academic use. ```python import wandb wandb.init( project="fraud-detection", name="rf-baseline", config={ # hyperparameters "model_type": "RandomForest", "n_estimators": 300, "max_depth": 12, "data_version": data_hash, }, tags=["baseline", "tabular"], ) for epoch in range(n_epochs): wandb.log({"train_loss": train_loss, "val_loss": val_loss, "val_f1": val_f1, "epoch": epoch}) wandb.log({ "confusion_matrix": wandb.plot.confusion_matrix( probs=None, y_true=y_val, preds=y_pred, class_names=["legit", "fraud"]), "roc": wandb.plot.roc_curve(y_val, y_prob_2d, labels=["legit", "fraud"]), }) wandb.finish() ``` Its distinctive feature is **sweeps** — built-in hyperparameter search with automatic tracking: ```python sweep_config = { "method": "bayes", # or "grid", "random" "metric": {"name": "val_f1", "goal": "maximize"}, "parameters": { "n_estimators": {"values": [100, 300, 500]}, "max_depth": {"min": 3, "max": 20}, "min_samples_leaf": {"min": 1, "max": 30}, "learning_rate": {"distribution": "log_uniform_values", "min": 1e-4, "max": 1e-1}, }, "early_terminate": {"type": "hyperband", "min_iter": 5}, } sweep_id = wandb.sweep(sweep_config, project="fraud-detection") wandb.agent(sweep_id, function=train_one_config, count=50) ``` Bayesian search learns from previous runs to focus on promising regions, and hyperband early-terminates unpromising configurations. The dashboard then produces a **parallel coordinates plot** showing which hyperparameters actually mattered — frequently revealing that two of your five parameters drive everything and the rest are noise. | | MLflow | Weights & Biases | |---|---|---| | Hosting | Self-hosted or local | Cloud (self-host on enterprise) | | Cost | Free, open source | Free personal, paid teams | | Dashboard | Functional | Excellent | | Model registry | **Strong** | Artifacts + model registry | | Sweeps | External (Optuna) | **Built in** | | Deployment integration | **Strong** | Weaker | | Offline use | **Yes** | Limited | The practical choice: **MLflow when you need self-hosting, an offline environment or tight deployment integration; W&B when collaboration, sweeps and visualization matter most.** Many teams use both — W&B for experimentation, MLflow for the production registry. ##### Comparing and reproducing runs The payoff arrives when you query your experiment history: ```python runs = mlflow.search_runs( experiment_names=["fraud-detection"], filter_string="metrics.f1 > 0.85 and params.model_type = 'RandomForest'", order_by=["metrics.f1 DESC"], max_results=10, ) print(runs[["run_id", "params.max_depth", "params.n_estimators", "metrics.f1", "params.git_commit"]]) ``` That query is exactly what the opening story needed. The 0.91 run would have its git commit, data hash, full parameter set and the serialized model itself — all recoverable in one command. Reproducing a run then becomes mechanical: ```python run = mlflow.get_run(run_id) print("Checkout commit:", run.data.params["git_commit"]) print("Data version:", run.data.params["data_version"]) print("Params:", {k: v for k, v in run.data.params.items() if k not in ("git_commit", "data_version")}) model = mlflow.sklearn.load_model(f"runs:/{run_id}/model") # or just load it directly ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Training script] --> B[Log params
+ git commit
+ data hash] B --> C[Train] C --> D[Log metrics
per epoch] D --> E[Log artifacts
model, plots, report] E --> F[(Tracking store)] F --> G[Dashboard:
compare, sort, filter] G --> H{Best run?} H --> I[Register model
+ set alias] I --> J[Production loads
by alias] F --> K[Reproduce:
checkout commit,
same data, same params] ``` ##### Common mistakes - **Not logging the data version** — the most common reason a result cannot be reproduced. - **Not logging the git commit**, so you do not know which code ran. - **Logging only the final metric** rather than per-epoch, losing the learning curve. - **Not saving the model artifact**, so a good run leaves nothing usable. - **Vague run names** — `run_1`, `run_2` — rather than descriptive ones. - **No tags**, making a hundred runs unfilterable. - **Logging secrets** into parameters, since these dashboards are often shared. - **Tracking only successful runs** — failures are informative, and knowing what did not work prevents repeating it. - **Starting tracking late**, after the interesting experiments are gone. - **No random seed logged**, so even identical parameters produce different results. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **instrument a training script with MLflow or W&B**, logging hyperparameters and metrics across several runs, then compare them in the dashboard. Deliberately run five configurations rather than one — the dashboard is worthless with a single run, and the moment it becomes valuable is when you sort five by F1 and immediately see which parameter mattered. The mini project is a **hyperparameter sweep with a report identifying the best configuration**. Use W&B sweeps or Optuna with MLflow. The report is the deliverable: state the best configuration, its score, **and which hyperparameters actually mattered** — a parallel coordinates plot usually shows that two of your five parameters drive nearly all the variance, which is genuinely useful for the next project. For the assignment, **explain why experiment tracking is essential for reproducibility and list what to log for every run**. Use the failure mode as your argument: an ML result depends on parameters, data version, code version, seed and environment, and a screenshot captures one of those five. Then give the full logging checklist from the table above, and emphasize the two that people omit — data version and git commit — because those are precisely the ones whose absence makes a result permanently unrecoverable. ##### Key takeaways - ML results depend on far more than hyperparameters — data version, code commit, seed and environment all matter, and memory captures none of them. - Log parameters, per-epoch metrics, data version, git commit, artifacts and tags on every run, including the failures. - MLflow is free, local-first and strong on the model registry; W&B has a better dashboard and built-in sweeps — many teams use both. - Register production models by alias rather than version number so promotion and rollback are registry changes, not code deployments. - The payoff is queryable history: filtering runs by metric and recovering the exact commit, data and parameters that produced a result.
